title: The Screenish Inquisition: The Newest Excuse Not to Reform Education
author: Stefan Bauschard
summary: Stefan Bauschard argues that the wave of state phone-ban legislation functions as a scapegoat that lets schools avoid harder structural reforms. He traces the argument through a motte-and-bailey move he calls 'screenwashing,' in which a defensible claim ('some apps distract some kids') gets swapped for an indefensible one ('technology broke the schools'), and marshals research, including a 350,000-student well-being analysis, the University of Birmingham phone-ban study, and PISA 2022, to show that device effects are small, inconsistent, and dependent entirely on how adults design their use. He contends the ban is popular precisely because it is free: it requires no new funding, no retraining, no schedule change, and no accountability for the underlying problems of teacher pay, chronic absenteeism, rigid seat-time structures, and a widening achievement gap between top and bottom performers. The piece closes with a constructive agenda, tool fluency as a taught literacy, project-based and oral-communication-heavy assessment, better pay and planning time for teachers, arguing that the ban addresses none of it.
points: Bauschard's central claim, backed by a 350,000-adolescent meta-analysis, is that screen time explains at most 0.4 percent of variation in adolescent well-being, roughly the same as eating potatoes, undercutting the causal story behind bans.

He names the rhetorical move driving policy as 'screenwashing': trading a defensible claim (some apps distract, some edtech underdelivered) for an indefensible one (technology broke the schools) to avoid confronting funding, staffing, and pedagogy failures.

The University of Birmingham's 30-school randomized-style study found no measurable difference in wellbeing, sleep, or attainment between phone-ban and phone-permissive schools, while ban enforcement consumed over 100 staff hours weekly.

PISA 2022 data shows device use cuts both ways depending on adult design: up to an hour of learning-focused device use correlated with a 14-point math score gain, while classmate device distraction correlated with a 15-point loss.

His 'Waldorf Astoria effect' argument reframes screen-free schooling as a class privilege: affluent kids get tech fluency at home regardless of school policy, while lower-income students lose their only structured path to becoming builders rather than consumers of technology.
quotes: We handed it to the kids with no instruction, and then acted betrayed when they used it as a slot machine.
The word for the move is screenwashing: washing your hands of a systemic problem by pointing at a screen.

The largest analysis of the screen-time literature, 350,000 adolescents across three datasets, found that digital technology use explains at most 0.4 percent of the variation in well-being, roughly the same association as eating potatoes.

The first nationally representative study of school phone bans, from the University of Birmingham across 30 English schools, found no difference in well-being, sleep, or attainment between restrictive and permissive schools.

And PISA 2022 found that students who used devices for up to an hour a day of learning in school scored 14 points higher in math than those who used none, while students distracted by classmates' devices scored 15 points lower.
The phone is in use a median of 43 minutes a school day. The school day runs roughly 400. If the phone is stealing 43 minutes, who is responsible for the other 357?
Teachers earned 26.9 percent less per week in 2024 than similarly educated professionals, the widest gap in three decades of tracking. A ban is cheaper than a raise.
Ban the phones if you must. Then do the work. Teach the tools. Ask the kids. Pay the adults. Fund the ones who are falling behind.
